title: Stroke, haemorrhage and cerebrovascular disease

steps.tx: Non-contrast computed tomography remains the first-line imaging modality for suspected **acute ischaemic stroke**. The **hyperdense middle cerebral artery sign** indicates acute intraluminal thromboembolism within the horizontal M1 segment, demonstrating exceptional specificity for large vessel occlusion before parenchymal changes manifest on early brain scans.

steps.tx: The **ASPECTS** (Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score) system quantifies early ischemic changes across the **middle cerebral artery** territory. Scoring starts at 10 points on baseline non-contrast CT, subtracting 1 point for each involved region among subcortical structures and cortical zones across defined axial slices.

steps.tx: On magnetic resonance imaging, acute cellular injury produces marked restriction of microscopic water movement. High **diffusion-weighted imaging** signal paired with low **apparent diffusion coefficient** values reflects acute **cytotoxic oedema** resulting from energetic failure of ATP-dependent sodium-potassium pumps in ischaemic neurons and glia.

High diffusion-weighted imaging signal paired with low apparent diffusion coefficient values reflects acute cytotoxic oedema resulting from energetic failure of ATP-dependent sodium-potassium pumps in ischaemic neurons and glia.

steps.tx: Advanced perfusion assessment identifies tissue salvageable by revascularisation therapy. A critical **CT perfusion mismatch** defines the **ischaemic penumbra**, characterised by delayed transit time (Tmax > 6 seconds or MTT > 145%) alongside preserved **cerebral blood volume** (CBV > 2.0 mL/100g) in viable hypoperfused tissue.
steps.say: Advanced perfusion assessment identifies tissue salvageable by revascularisation therapy. A critical CT perfusion mismatch defines the ischaemic penumbra, characterised by delayed transit time exceeding 6 seconds alongside preserved cerebral blood volume above 2.0 millilitres per 100 grams in viable hypoperfused tissue.

steps.tx: Non-contrast computed tomography promptly identifies acute intracranial extravasation. **Subarachnoid haemorrhage** manifests as hyperdense blood filling the basal cisterns and cerebral sulci, most frequently originating from the rupture of a saccular aneurysm situated at the **anterior communicating artery** complex in the anterior Circle of Willis.

steps.tx: Intracranial microbleeds exhibit characteristic spatial patterns that separate chronic vasculopathies on gradient echo or susceptibility-weighted sequences. Chronic hypertension damages small perforating arterioles, producing punctate lesions confined to the **putamen**, thalamus, and pons, whereas **cerebral amyloid angiopathy** yields strictly lobar cortical-subcortical microbleeds.

steps.tx: Cervical arterial trauma or spontaneous shear forces create an intramural entry tear. Non-traumatic dissection of the **internal carotid artery** produces an eccentric crescent of hyperintense subacute **mural haematoma** surrounding an attenuated eccentric lumen, optimally visualised on fat-saturated T1-weighted axial magnetic resonance images.

steps.tx: Thrombosis of the cerebral venous collector pathways presents with intracranial hypertension and atypical venous infarction. On contrast-enhanced computed tomography, **venous sinus thrombosis** classically produces the **empty delta sign**, characterised by a central non-enhancing triangular thrombus surrounded by vivid collateral enhancement of the engorged dural leaves.
